guideTitle: Best Immersion Blenders with Food Processors (2026)
metaTitle: Best Immersion Blenders with Food Processors
metaDescription: Seven stick blenders that include a chopper or food processor bowl, compared on motor, speed control, attachments and cleanup for soups, sauces and prep.
expertTake: The Cuisinart stick blender with a 4-cup food processor attachment is the top pick, because the processor bowl slices, shreds and chops, which most chopper-bowl kits cannot. The Mueller 800-watt 5-in-1 is the value pick for a full toolkit at a low tier. If you want to process large volumes of vegetables or dough, skip kits like these and buy a standalone processor.
introParagraphs: A stick blender that doubles as a small food processor promises a lot in one drawer. The motor sits in the handle, and a bowl with a blade swaps on for chopping, which saves counter space and a separate appliance.

The reality is that these kits split into two kinds: those with a true processor bowl and discs, and those with a simple chopper bowl. We sorted the seven by which kind they are, then compared motor power, speed control and how well each handles hot soup and cold prep.

products.name: Cuisinart Variable Speed Immersion Blender with Food Processor

specList.label: Blending shaft
specList.value: Detachable with stainless blade and guard

products.description:
This kit has the one thing most of its rivals lack: a real processor bowl that slices and shreds as well as chops. The four-cup bowl, with discs, turns the stick blender motor into a small food processor for vegetables and cheese. That makes it the most complete answer to the idea of one motor, many jobs.

The blending shaft is detachable and has a stainless steel blade with a guard, so it works in a pot or a jar for soups and sauces. Variable speed control lets you start slowly to limit splatter. Compared with the 3-cup chopper in the Cuisinart CSB-179, you gain slicing and shredding and lose some portability.

Plan on small batches in the processor bowl, because four cups is not a full-size machine. Rinse the shaft right after blending, wash the processor parts by hand and store the discs together. Keep the motor body dry and never submerge it. Feed soft vegetables through the slicing disc first and harder ones second, since a small motor handles a light load better than a dense one right at the start. Let the motor rest between rounds, because stick blender motors are built for short bursts rather than long runs.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want soup blending plus real slicing and shredding from one motor.
pros: Processor bowl slices and shreds, not just chops
Detachable shaft with stainless blade guard
cons: More parts to wash and store

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 7 3-in-1 Stick Blender and Processor
products.description:
The Braun's identity is control. Easy SmartSpeed has no preset speeds: you press harder for faster, and the motor follows your hand, so the whole thing works with one hand. It suits cooks who find speed dials fiddly and want to feel the blend.

The ACTIVEBlade design uses a flexible shaft that moves the blade up and down as you blend, which is meant to give finer results in less time. The kit pairs the blender with a processor bowl for chopping. Beside the Cuisinart, the Braun puts more of its effort into the blending end than into a processor bowl with discs.

Because it is a precise tool, treat it with care. Do not run the blade dry or lift it out of liquid while spinning, rinse the shaft immediately after soup and store the processor bowl with its blade seated. The maker cites a sales ranking, which is a marketing claim rather than a performance figure. In use, the real test is how it handles a pot of hot tomato soup, where the flexible shaft keeps the blade moving through chunks instead of pushing them aside.
products.bestFor: People who want intuitive one-handed speed control and smooth blending.
pros: ACTIVEBlade moves up and down for finer results
cons: No fixed speeds to repeat a setting
Processor bowl is a chopper-style accessory

products.name: Cuisinart CSB-179 Smart Stick with 3-Cup Chopper
products.description:
The CSB-179 is the quiet one. A 300-watt DC motor drives an 8-inch stainless steel blending arm, and the listing stresses its low noise. A variable speed control sweeps from low to high, with a push button for continuous or pulse running.

The kit includes a 3-cup chopper and grinder for herbs, nuts and breadcrumbs, plus a whisk for eggs and cream. It is a chopper rather than a full processor, so it cannot slice or shred. For cooks who want a tidy, quiet kit for soups and small chopping, it fits well.

The lower wattage compared with the 800-watt Mueller means it is gentler on dense loads. Blend in the pot, keep the blade submerged and rinse the arm right away. Wash the chopper bowl by hand and keep the whisk attachment dry before storing. The grinder blade is meant for herbs, nuts and breadcrumbs, so toast nuts lightly and cool them before grinding, since warm nuts turn to paste. A quiet motor also makes it a considerate choice for early-morning smoothies or a household with a sleeping baby.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prize low noise and a simple kit for soups and small chopping.

products.name: Bonsenkitchen 4-in-1 Immersion Blender with Processor
products.description:
A 500-watt high-torque motor and twelve speeds plus a turbo button put this kit in the middle of the pack. The twelve fixed speeds let you land on the same texture every time, which suits those who like to repeat a recipe. The body is stainless steel and designed to resist splashes.

The four functions include a food processor attachment, which in this class is usually a chopper-style bowl. Think sauces, dressings and chopped aromatics. Against the 800-watt Mueller, it gives up some power but keeps the speed range.

Use the turbo button sparingly, because it is a burst of power that can throw splatter. Keep the blade in the liquid, rinse the shaft after use and wash the processor bowl in warm soapy water. Dry the stainless body to avoid spots. If you plan to blend a lot of hot liquid, vent the container and keep a towel nearby, because any stick blender can throw steam and droplets when lifted out too early.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want repeatable fixed speeds and a middle-of-the-road motor.

products.name: Mueller 800W 5-in-1 Immersion Blender with Chopper

specList.label: Tools
specList.value: Blending arm, chopper, whisk, frother, beaker

products.description:
This kit puts five tools on one 800-watt motor: a blending arm, a chopper bowl, a whisk, a frother and a 20-ounce beaker. The listing highlights frozen fruit blending, and the 800 watts gives it more headroom than the 300-watt and 500-watt kits.

Twelve set speeds plus a turbo button mean no guesswork, and you can chop onions and salsa in the chopper bowl, whip cream with the whisk and puree soup in the pot. It is the value pick because it gives a complete toolkit for little money.

The chopper is a small bowl and does not slice or shred. Treat frozen fruit in small pieces and add liquid first, then blend in the beaker with the head tilted so the blade draws fruit down from the sides. Run it in bursts of ten to fifteen seconds with short rests, because even an 800-watt motor heats when pushed through a solid frozen load. Wash the beaker and chopper bowl by hand, rinse the arm straight away and store the pieces together in the beaker.
products.bestFor: Budget cooks who want a full five-tool kit and more motor than the mid-power kits.
pros: 800 W motor in a low-cost kit
Five tools and a 20 oz beaker
cons: Many small parts to keep together

products.name: KOIOS 1000W 5-in-1 Immersion Blender Set
products.description:
At 1000 watts this is one of the strongest motors in the guide, and a 304 stainless steel shaft is designed to be anti-splash. It fits most pots, mason jars and wide-mouth cups, which makes it easy to blend in what you already own. The five-in-one kit replaces a blender, chopper, whisk, frother and beaker.

Low speeds are intended for gentle blending and high speeds for tough loads, with twelve speeds and a turbo boost. Beside the Mueller 800-watt kit, it adds raw power. As with every kit in this guide, the chopper is a small bowl and not a slicing machine.

High power calls for discipline. Start on a low speed, keep the blade submerged and do not run it for long periods, because a hot motor wears faster. Rinse the shaft immediately, wash the chopper by hand and dry the stainless to avoid spots.
products.bestFor: Cooks who blend thick soups and frozen drinks and want the most power in a kit.
pros: 1000 W is the strongest motor here
cons: High power needs careful speed control

products.name: Turelar 1100W 5-in-1 Corded Immersion Blender Set
products.description:
The Turelar leads on paper with an 1100-watt full copper motor. A variable-speed trigger with a pulse-activated sensor lets you control the speed with your finger, which is intuitive for hot soups where you want to ramp up gradually. A food-grade nylon blade guard minimizes suction and protects your pots from scratches.

The five-in-one set includes the usual chopper, whisk and beaker. As with the other kits, the chopper is not a slicing processor. The high wattage gives it extra headroom on thick loads, but the motor and body are lighter than a full-size machine.

With so much power, pulse the trigger and work in short bursts. Keep the blade fully submerged, clean the nylon guard after each use and store the set in its beaker. Replace the guard if it cracks. For thick soups, lift the head slightly and tilt the pot so the blade can move through the whole batch instead of stalling in a pocket of vegetables.
products.bestFor: Cooks who prefer a trigger-style control and a protective nylon guard for nonstick pots.
cons: Maximum wattage is a headline, not a day-to-day need

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Cuisinart with a 4-cup processor slices and shreds, while the Mueller, KOIOS, Bonsen and Turelar kits include a chopper bowl that only chops. If you want slicing and shredding, only the first is a real processor. Check the discs before you buy.

The range here runs from the 300-watt Cuisinart CSB-179 to the 1100-watt Turelar, with the 500-watt Bonsen, 800-watt Mueller and 1000-watt KOIOS in between. Higher wattage helps with thick soups and frozen fruit. It does not make the chopper bowl slice.

The Braun uses pressure-based SmartSpeed, the Turelar uses a trigger and the Mueller, KOIOS and Bonsen use twelve fixed speeds plus turbo. Fixed speeds repeat; pressure control is intuitive. Pick the one that suits how you cook.
The Cuisinart CSB-179 has an 8-inch stainless arm and the KOIOS has a 304 stainless anti-splash shaft. A longer shaft reaches deep stockpots. Stainless resists staining and odors better than plastic.

The Turelar's nylon guard and the stainless guards on the other kits protect nonstick pots from scratches to different degrees. A bare metal guard can scrape a coated pan if you press it to the bottom. If you blend in the pot, choose a kit with a plastic or nylon guard and lift the head slightly off the surface.
Whisk, frother, beaker and chopper bowl come in the five-in-one kits. Count how many you will use before paying for them. A whisk and chopper cover most people.

specDecoder.meaning: A handheld motor with a blade at the end of a shaft, used inside a pot or jar. It blends without pouring.
specDecoder.watchFor: All seven here share this core, with different add-ons.

specDecoder.meaning: A bowl with a blade, and sometimes discs, that mounts on the motor. A real processor slices and shreds; a chopper only chops.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Cuisinart with a 4-cup bowl lists slice and shred.

specDecoder.meaning: A trigger whose pressure sets the speed. It gives a smooth ramp.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Turelar and Cuisinart use this style.

specDecoder.meaning: A burst button that runs the motor at full speed for a short time.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Mueller, KOIOS and Bonsen offer turbo.

specDecoder.meaning: A cover over the blade that limits suction and protects cookware. It also reduces splatter.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Turelar lists a nylon guard.

howWeEvaluated.title: Processor versus chopper
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether each kit includes a real processor bowl or only a chopper. Slicing and shredding capability ranked highest. Chopper-only kits were graded as chopping tools.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 300, 500, 800, 1000 and 1100 watts with their speed controls. Strong motors with fine control ranked higher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Soup and pot use
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered shaft length, blade guards and splash design, the features that matter when blending hot liquid in a pot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted tools, from whisks to beakers, and asked which are genuinely useful. Kits with fewer but better tools ranked well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at detachable shafts, stainless parts and how the kit stores. Detachable and dishwasher-friendly parts ranked higher.

cards.label: Real processor bowl
cards.text: The Cuisinart with a 4-cup processor slices and shreds. It suits cooks who want more than chopping.

cards.label: Chopper bowl
cards.text: The Mueller, KOIOS, Bonsen, Turelar and Braun chop and mince. They suit sauces, salsa and aromatics.

howToChoose.note: Pick the real processor if you slice or shred, and a chopper kit if you only chop and blend.

howToChoose.subheading: For Soup in the Pot Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A long shaft, a blade guard and splash design. Keep the blade submerged and start slowly. Let boiling soup cool a little.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The KOIOS with an anti-splash shaft and the Cuisinart CSB-179 with an 8-inch arm are the best fit.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want slicing and shredding or intuitive control. The Cuisinart with a processor or the Braun repays it.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You blend soups and chop small amounts. The Mueller or KOIOS does it for less.

maintenance.why: Soup and puree dry on the blade. A quick rinse in warm water prevents caking.
The motor body must not be submerged. Wipe it with a damp cloth only.
A cracked guard can scratch cookware. Replace it if it splits.
Sharp blades and plastic bowls last longer by hand. Store the lid separately.
Water spots and odors cling to wet steel. A dry cloth prevents them.

faq.q: Can an immersion blender replace a food processor?
faq.a: Not fully. A kit with a real processor bowl, like the Cuisinart, covers slicing and shredding in small amounts. Chopper-bowl kits only chop. For big batches or dough, a standalone processor is better.

faq.q: Which kit has the most power?
faq.a: The Turelar lists 1100 watts and the KOIOS 1000. The Mueller has 800, Bonsen 500 and Cuisinart CSB-179 300. More watts help with thick loads.
Not necessarily. Fixed speeds repeat well, while pressure or trigger control is intuitive. Choose the style that you find easiest to use.
Yes, in the pot, with the blade submerged. Start slowly and let boiling soup cool a little. A blade guard protects nonstick pots.

faq.q: Are the chopper bowls dishwasher safe?
faq.a: Check the manual. Hand washing is the safest way to protect the blade and plastic. Never submerge the motor.
If you value one-handed intuitive control, yes. It has no fixed speeds, so it is less repeatable. It suits cooks who blend by feel.
